extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of media studies, sociology, and communication; researchers analyzing mediatization
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and conceptual criteria for analysing how media intervene in social interaction and institutions (mediatization). Emphasises dimensions such as mediated vs non-mediated interaction, media logic, institutional autonomy, virtualization, and geographic/scale tensions (global/local, homogenization/differentiation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mediated vs non-mediated communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than adopting earlier three-fold terminology, it is more satisfactory to distinguish between non-mediated (face-to-face) and mediated communication and then to specify the subcategories in terms of parameters like one-way/two-way, interpersonal/mass, text/audio/visual, and so forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify interactions first as face-to-face or mediated, then characterise mediated forms by parameters (one-way/two-way, interpersonal/mass, modality). Use these parameters to compare affordances and limits of different media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess media's extension of interaction in time and space
rubrics_metrics.description: Media can extend interaction in time and space: media allow instant communication with individuals anywhere in the world. Mediated interaction does not require the parties to be in the same space at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure how a medium decouples co-presence (temporal and spatial extension), and analyse consequences for coordination, reach, and synchronous/asynchronous possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate changes to stage/backstage dynamics and impression management
rubrics_metrics.description: Because mediated interaction takes place between individuals who do not share the same physical space, media change the ability of actors to steer how the social situation is defined, to steer verbal/non-verbal communication and accessories, and to define territorial boundaries in the interaction. There is an essential imbalance between an individual’s ability to manage the impression he makes and others’ ability to examine it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at how media narrow or widen channels (easier impression management with narrower channels like SMS/email), how backstage becomes accessible or reconfigured, and how senders manage timing and image (e.g., delayed responses, curated self-presentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure multitasking and parallel-stage participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Media make it considerably easier for individuals to ‘act’ on several stages simultaneously; participants can keep several social interactions going at the same time (e.g., talking to family while watching television; web windows open to multiple interactions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the medium’s affordances for simultaneous interactions and the degree to which users can divide attention across scenes; consider design features (background play, glanceable notifications) that enable multitasking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess media as means to optimize social interaction (control and lowered investment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media allow actors to optimize social interaction to their own advantage by lightening the burden of social relations and permitting greater control over the exchange of information (e.g., email lets you steer interaction more than in-person conversation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how a medium reduces required social effort (time, emotional labour, cost) and how it increases sender control (timing of replies, edited messages); consider trade-offs with social norms and reciprocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse norm-enforcing mechanism transformations (facework, gossip, ridicule, scolding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediated interaction changes mutual relations and norms; norm-regulating mechanisms in face-to-face encounters (deference, facework to avoid embarrassment) are transformed: gossip, ridicule and scolding can take new forms and may be more publicly accessible via media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate how media change the acceptability, visibility and consequences of norm enforcement (e.g., gossip spread via blogs, reality TV, SMS-based mockery, online mobbing), including effects on dignity and group cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate de-linking of place-bound social contexts and virtual ‘stage’ formation
rubrics_metrics.description: The medium links different physical localities and social contexts in a single interactive space, but it does not do away with the reality of the separate place-bound contexts; users’ place-bound contexts may assume the character of ‘backstage’ relative to mediated interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how media connect disparate physical contexts into one mediated interaction space, how users negotiate multiple social contexts, and how this de-linking affects privacy, accountability and cross-context exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify media’s functions on the macrosocial level (interfaces, shared experience, public sphere)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three functions of media on the macro level: (1) they constitute an interface in the relations within and between institutions; (2) they constitute a realm of shared experience offering a presentation and interpretation of ‘the way things are’; (3) they help create a political public sphere where institutions pursue and defend interests and legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing media-institution relations, score or describe media’s role as (a) interface/resource for institutional interaction, (b) provider of collective frames/experience, and (c) arena for political/public contestation and legitimacy-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use field/autonomy framework (Bourdieu) to measure mediatization
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of mediatization may be measured according to how much a field’s autonomous pole has weakened relative to its heteronomous pole; media too have autonomous (professional journalism, codes of ethics) and heteronomous (advertising market) poles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess shifts in a field by measuring influence from media (and other fields): quantify or describe weakening of field-specific criteria/values and increasing dependence on media logics or markets. Consider both directions of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect tensions between journalistic ideals and commercial/political pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: In news media, journalistic criteria of news value and ideals of good journalism often compete with demands to sell copies and influence from news sources (commercialization, politicization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate instances where economic or political incentives shape content or processes, noting departures from professional norms; use examples like advertising influence or source-driven reporting as indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess media’s metacapital and ideological power
rubrics_metrics.description: Media's metacapital: the ability of media to form categories used across fields to interpret the world; media can present themselves as the centre of society and provide interpretive positions and categorical frameworks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse the extent to which media define salient categories (cognitive, social, lexical) that structure public understanding, and consider whether media descriptions become taken-for-granted 'natural' ways to comprehend social reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure creation of a shared experiential world (re-embedding/disembedding)
rubrics_metrics.description: One principal consequence of mediatization is the constitution of a shared experiential world; media create a common horizon of experience across institutions, sometimes eroding local cultures in favor of national or transnational realms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reach and penetration of media-generated common frames (national rituals, celebrity events, blockbuster culture) and their impact on local cultures; consider historical comparisons (printing, radio, TV, internet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate virtualization and domestication of institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediatization leads to virtualization of social institutions (politics, education, art no longer strictly place-bound) and domestication (the home/family becomes the pivot for access to other institutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse how institutional participation is decoupled from place (e.g., home access to politics via TV/internet), how homes absorb institutional functions (home offices, domestic media consumption), and implications for regulation of behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh centrifugal vs centripetal and homogenization vs differentiation tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The media landscape produces contradictory tendencies: centrifugal (globalization, transnational flows) and centripetal (localization, neighborhood media); homogenization (global blockbusters) and differentiation (segmented niches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a given phenomenon, map which tendencies predominate (globalizing vs localizing; homogenizing vs fragmenting). Use examples (Al-Jazeera, Da Vinci Code, blogging, online gaming, local radio) to illustrate each pole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine coupling strength between media and institutions (loose couplings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Links between local, national, individual/group-oriented and global are less stable and resemble loose couplings; in globalized media systems the linking mechanism between media representations and social action is less pronounced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate how tightly media outputs translate into institutional/policy changes in different contexts; identify arenas where media debate has marginal vs direct influence on decision-making, and consider network governance implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological criterion: empirically investigate mediatization in context
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which and how media logic affects any given institution, the mutual interaction of institutions, and society as a whole will vary, and these are questions for empirical investigation. Any empirical analysis of mediatization should enquire whether, and to what extent, other institutions stand to win or lose autonomy in relation to other fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design empirical studies that assess historical and cultural context, measure autonomy changes, and separate mediatization effects from commercialization or politicization. Use field-theory-informed indicators and comparative cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for segmentation and occasional collective media events
rubrics_metrics.description: The proliferation of channels leads to segmentation and fewer programs that everyone encounters together; nevertheless, occasional media phenomena (royal events, blockbuster releases) can momentarily revive a collective 'we'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure audience fragmentation (niche communities, chat rooms, online games) against indicators of mass collective events (ratings spikes, national rituals) to understand the balance between segmentation and shared moments.
